items.title: Training decision models for simulating human respondents
items.desc: Shows that fine-tuning language models on historical respondent-level choice data lowers treatment-effect error by 22% to 89% when they are used as synthetic survey respondents on four held-out studies; a small trained model beat a much larger off-the-shelf one on three of the four. [arXiv cs.CL, submitted 2026-11-23]

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Welcome back. Today a paper on using language models as stand-in survey respondents, and a fix for their bias. We should say up front that we're working from the abstract only.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: Researchers increasingly use language models as synthetic respondents in market research, conjoint analysis and randomized experiments. The trouble is that choices generated by off-the-shelf models bias the econometric estimates you then compute from them.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: And the authors say neither proprietary models nor more reasoning effort reliably cures that bias. So what do they try?

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: They train the model on choices. They update the weights of a model on historical respondent-level choice microdata, using conditional maximum likelihood, before inference and without any data from the target study.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: They train on two discrete choice experiments, then test on four held-out studies from new domains: vaccines, nutrition labels, consumer rights and AI, with new response formats too.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: The headline: across three model scales, choice training cuts treatment-effect error by between 22 and 89 percent. And a small choice-trained model beats a much larger off-the-shelf model on three of the four studies.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: There's a caveat, though. Training on a single study lowers cross-entropy but can actually make treatment-effect error worse, so more fit to one study isn't automatically better.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: The takeaway: choice training gives a stronger starting point for estimating human preferences, and it complements calibration done after inference.

items.title: Burning the Bridge: Agentification and Domestic Value Added
items.desc: Theoretical model of a small open economy in which firms replace local work with foreign AI agents: extending agent use in local services can lower domestic value added and consumption once wages hit a reservation floor, while exporters can offset the loss; calibrated with Brazilian and Mexican accounts. [arXiv econ.GN, submitted 2026-11-23]

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Today's paper asks whether swapping local workers for foreign AI agents can leave a country poorer even while firms get more productive. This is based on the abstract only.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: The setup is a small open economy where exporters and local service firms both use AI agents. A firm can produce more per paid hour yet generate less income at home, because the agent's fee leaves the country.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: So where does it bite?

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: Once wages reach a reservation floor, extending agent use in local services lowers domestic income at unchanged foreign costs. Value added and consumption can fall too, if the suppliers capture enough of the savings.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Exporters have an offset. Adopting agents can expand production and earn the foreign exchange needed to pay for them.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: The paper puts numbers on it using Brazilian accounts. A supplier bargaining share above about 0.15 is enough to make more local-service adoption reduce value added, even at negligible foreign costs. For tradables the threshold is about 0.66.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: There's also a dynamic worry: as domestic capabilities decline, returning to local production gets more expensive, so suppliers can charge more at renewal.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: The takeaway: who captures the gains from AI agents, and whether the sector earns foreign exchange, decides whether adoption helps or hurts a national economy.

items.title: Adopting AI Technologies without Traps: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Framework
items.desc: Proposes a multi-agent Markov decision process framework with human and AI agents to find optimal AI adoption strategies, modeling harms such as skill erosion as negative transitions or rewards; applied to AI offloading, firm workforce structure and human-AI employment equilibria. [arXiv cs.AI, submitted 2026-11-23]

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: This paper builds a reinforcement learning framework for deciding how to adopt AI without falling into traps. We're working from the abstract only here.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: The traps are things like lost jobs and training opportunities, or declining cognitive skills, set against the immediate productivity rewards of using AI.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: How do they model that?

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: As a multi-agent Markov decision process with both human and AI agents. Negative effects show up as undesirable state transitions or negative rewards.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: The key idea is that adding AI doesn't just raise immediate rewards. It also changes the states of the humans and AI agents involved.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: They apply it to three problems: AI offloading that leads to skill erosion, the best human resource structure for a firm adopting AI, and economic equilibria in trading and employment between humans and AI.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: The abstract doesn't give numerical results, so this is a framework paper.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: The takeaway: use dynamic, long-horizon models, not only one-period gains, when deciding how much to lean on AI.

items.title: Delta-Vega Hedging with Deep Reinforcement Learning: From Simulation to Reality
items.desc: Trains a PPO reinforcement-learning agent on simulated stochastic-volatility data to hedge price and volatility risk with the underlying plus a longer-dated option under transaction costs; on historical S&P 500 option data two-instrument strategies roughly halve P&L dispersion versus Delta hedging and PPO beats Delta-Vega on P&L volatility. [arXiv q-fin.CP, submitted 2026-11-24]

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Today, deep reinforcement learning for hedging options. Abstract-only again.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: Hedging with just the underlying leaves you exposed to changes in volatility. You can trade a second option to cover that, but at higher transaction costs.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: So the authors train an agent with proximal policy optimization on synthetic data from a stochastic volatility model. It trades the underlying and a longer-dated option, and sees only market-observable quantities so the policy transfers to real data.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: In simulation, it matches the Delta-Vega benchmark at baseline costs and increasingly outperforms it as costs rise.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: On historical S&P 500 index option data, the two-instrument strategies roughly halve the profit and loss dispersion of a plain Delta hedge, and the agent gets lower profit and loss volatility than Delta-Vega at comparable costs.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: Its advantage is concentrated in high-volatility episodes.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: The takeaway: a policy trained only on simulations can carry over to real option markets, especially when costs and volatility are high.

items.title: AgentBank: Banking on Blockchain Agentic Payments
items.desc: Proposes a smart-contract banking layer so AI agents can pay for data and compute from pooled funds under owner mandates and spending limits; experiments show 52-77% less idle liquidity than per-agent wallets, and the paper examines reserve policy and automated bank-run risk. [arXiv cs.CR, submitted 2026-11-24]

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Today: a bank for AI agents. Abstract-only.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: AI agents increasingly pay for data and computation using protocols like x402 and AP2, but giving each agent its own wallet means idle money and an asset transfer for every payment.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: AgentBank is a smart-contract layer where agents spend bank liabilities under owner-issued mandates and on-chain spending limits. Internal payments just update balances.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: Pooled backing funds are split between reserves and yield-bearing strategies, which raises the question of reserves.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: The authors bound losses from compromised agent keys and analyze how correlated demand affects reserve requirements.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: Experiments show idle liquidity falls by 52 to 77 percent versus per-agent wallets, and gas costs fall for batched payments. They also use historical decentralized finance liquidity data to study stress, and look at automated bank runs.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Why does this matter? If software agents become routine buyers of data and computing, how their money is held and moved becomes a real design question, not an afterthought.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: And the abstract is candid that pooling concentrates risk. A compromised key or a correlated rush of withdrawals is exactly what the reserve analysis tries to bound.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: The takeaway: pooling helps efficiency, but it brings old banking risks to machine payments.

items.title: Pretrained Tabular Features and the Measurement of Financial Proximity
items.desc: Uses frozen representations of four tabular foundation models as a measure of firm dissimilarity in a spatial asset-pricing model of US equities, 2011-2025; their gains over a direct distance on the same disclosures turn consistently positive once broad SEC filing data are included. [arXiv q-fin.PR, submitted 2026-11-23]

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: This paper treats the insides of tabular foundation models as a measuring tool for finance. Abstract-only.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: Spatial arbitrage pricing theory lets returns spill over between connected firms beyond common risk factors. The question is how to measure which firms are close.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: The authors take the frozen internal representations of four tabular foundation models and use them as a dissimilarity measure in a spatial asset-pricing model of US equities from 2011 to 2025.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: They find the estimated gains over a direct distance between the same disclosures become consistently positive once broad SEC filing data are included.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: That reframes these models from black-box predictors into instruments for measuring economic structure, with uses in peer selection, risk attribution and network-based asset pricing.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: A useful point for regulated settings is explanation. Predictive accuracy alone isn't enough there, so a model whose internal representation is used as a measurement instrument is easier to defend than a pure black box.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Of course, we only have the abstract, so details like effect sizes, how the four models differ, and robustness checks are beyond what we can say here.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: The takeaway: what pretrained models know about firms may be worth studying in its own right.

items.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation and Parameter-Efficient Fine-tuning for Financial Question Answering: Evidence from the FinQA Benchmark
items.desc: Studies a self-hosted pipeline (layout-aware parsing, hybrid retrieval, re-ranking, citation-grounded generation with a 4B-parameter model) for numerical questions over S&P 500 earnings reports; retrieval lifts exact-match accuracy on FinQA from 17.2% to 64.4%. [SSRN, posted 2026-11-24]

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: A short one on grounding language models for finance questions. We're working from the abstract only.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: Asked cold, a 4-billion-parameter model solves only 17.2 percent of the FinQA benchmark of numerical questions over S&P 500 earnings reports.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: The paper asks where the accuracy of a grounded system comes from, and what it costs. The pipeline is self-hosted: layout-aware document parsing, hybrid dense and sparse retrieval, re-ranking, and citation-grounded generation.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: With retrieval, exact-match accuracy rises to 64.4 percent.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: That is a big jump, from roughly one in six questions solved to nearly two in three, and it comes from a small model running on the firm's own hardware rather than a giant hosted one.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: This matters for finance teams that can't send sensitive documents to outside services. The paper's framing is about where the accuracy comes from and what it costs, so cost is part of the question.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Since we only have the abstract, we can't speak to the ablations or the fine-tuning results the title mentions.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: The takeaway: evidence at inference time matters far more than model size for financial question answering.

briefing.speaker: A
briefing.text: Hi, I'm Alex, and this is the Daily AI Research Digest for November twenty-fifth, 2026. Today: new papers on AI and economies, finance and hedging, and a market where AI optimism is wobbling.

briefing.speaker: B
briefing.text: And I'm Sam. Let's start with papers. One arXiv paper asks how language models can serve as synthetic survey respondents without biasing estimates.

briefing.speaker: A
briefing.text: Right. Off-the-shelf models bias the results. The authors fine-tune on historical choice data, and report treatment-effect error falling by twenty-two to eighty-nine percent on held-out studies. A small trained model even beat a bigger off-the-shelf one on three of four.

briefing.speaker: B
briefing.text: Next, a theory paper called Burning the Bridge. It models a small open economy where firms replace local work with foreign AI agents.

briefing.speaker: A
briefing.text: The surprising result is that firms get more productive yet domestic income can fall, depending on how much of the saving suppliers capture. With Brazilian accounts, a bargaining share above about fifteen percent is enough to cause that in local services.

briefing.speaker: B
briefing.text: In finance, a deep reinforcement learning hedger trained on simulations. On historical S&P 500 option data, two-instrument strategies roughly halve profit and loss dispersion versus plain delta hedging.

briefing.speaker: A
briefing.text: And AgentBank, a banking layer so AI agents can pay for services from pooled funds. It cuts idle liquidity by fifty-two to seventy-seven percent, though the authors also study bank-run risk.

briefing.speaker: B
briefing.text: There's also an SSRN paper on financial question answering: retrieval raises a small model's accuracy on a finance benchmark from seventeen percent to sixty-four percent.

briefing.speaker: A
briefing.text: Now news. The Wall Street Journal reports Anthropic's shares fell below their offering price for a third straight session, and the Financial Times says that makes life harder for OpenAI's IPO.

briefing.speaker: B
briefing.text: The Journal also looks at what an AI bust would do to the US economy. Economists agree it would hurt, but not on how much.

briefing.speaker: A
briefing.text: The Economist says copper has become a proxy bet on the AI revolution, with the pitfalls that implies. And Bloomberg reports Asian data centers are trying to sell spare computing capacity to US buyers after Washington tightened rules on Nvidia chips for Chinese firms.

briefing.speaker: B
briefing.text: On the financing side, the Financial Times says Nscale could stay private as the sell-off threatens its thirty-five billion dollar IPO, and the UK pensions regulator worries schemes may not know their AI exposure.

briefing.speaker: A
briefing.text: That's it for today. Find every item and the audio explainers in the web archive. See you tomorrow.
